intro: The Canadarm2 is a seven-jointed arm that assembles, maintains, and captures free-flying resupply vehicles. The crew and ground control share the same machine, operating it from the Cupola workstation and via scripts, respectively.
lessons.0.title: The SSRMS is a walking arm, not a fixed crane
lessons.0.summary: Both ends function as end effectors, allowing it to move across a vehicle's surface by walking along grapples.
lessons.0.body.0: Official records of STS-100 state that the Canadarm2 was attached to the exterior of Destiny, walked to an electrical grapple, and performed the first robot-to-robot handoff with the Shuttle's arm. This operation was a prerequisite for the installation of Quest on the subsequent flight.
lessons.0.body.1: NASA's human-robot allocation report categorizes the ISS as having three arms: the SSRMS (Canadarm2), the SPDM (Dextre), and the JEMRMS (Kibo). The SSRMS uses fixtures compatible with many grapples, excluding those in the Russian segment.
lessons.0.body.2: The candidate curriculum explicitly includes robotics training for using this arm. The resupply vehicle capture minigame compresses the official routine operations: approach monitoring, grappling, and subsequent ground-controlled berthing.
lessons.0.facts.0.label: Attachment
lessons.0.facts.1.label: Peers
lessons.0.deepDive.title: Correct position alone is not enough for grasping
lessons.0.deepDive.body.0: Even if the end effector reaches the target position in three dimensions, a safe grasp is not possible if the approach speed and attitude relative to the grapple are not aligned. Multiple cameras are used because a single image can lead to misjudgments regarding depth and approach speed.
lessons.0.deepDive.body.1: The arm in this game is a conceptual model that uses iterative calculations to approach a target with seven links. It does not replicate the joint limits, structural deflection, collision avoidance, or control software of the actual hardware. The displayed tolerance values are game settings, but the experience allows you to practice the judgment of checking position, velocity, and attitude separately.
lessons.1.title: Seven joints provide redundancy, but also pose the trap of singularities
lessons.1.summary: Extra joints allow obstacle avoidance. However, when joints are fully extended, the hand may not move in the intended direction.
lessons.1.body.0: The SSRMS has seven joints corresponding to the shoulder, elbow, and wrist. It has one degree of freedom in excess of the six required for position and orientation, allowing for obstacle avoidance and the selection of different joint configurations. This redundancy works in reverse at singularities. When the elbow is fully extended, a small target movement for the hand requires large joint velocities.
lessons.1.body.1: Training enforces the practice of not looking only at the hand. One must consider shoulder clearance, interference with the truss, cables, and solar array wings. In official capture operations, ground control places the arm in a high-hover position in advance to eliminate singularities and interference before handing control to the crew.
lessons.1.body.2: Safing stops the motion, applies brakes, and rejects the next command. If in doubt, stop. The courage to keep moving does not earn points with this arm.
lessons.1.facts.0.label: Joints
lessons.1.facts.1.label: Hazards
lessons.2.title: The Latching End Effector is a grasping mouth
lessons.2.summary: Wires tighten around the grapple fixture to create a near-rigid connection. A shallow catch will escape in the next second.
lessons.2.body.0: Both ends of the SSRMS are Latching End Effectors (LEEs). They encircle the grapple fixtures (GFs) of visiting vehicles or Orbital Replacement Units and tighten with snare wires to form a structural connection. Official capture reports refer to this moment as 'capture,' distinguishing it from subsequent movement and berthing.
lessons.2.body.1: A good capture is performed only when the relative velocity is low, the alignment is within tolerance, and the relative attitude is stable. The minigame displays three cameras because depth cannot be seen with a single view.
lessons.2.body.2: It is not over once grasped. Brakes, rigidity, and power and data paths may pass through the LEE. The fact that it walked to an electrical grapple in STS-100 is because the mouth can also function as a foot.
lessons.2.facts.0.label: Connection
lessons.2.facts.1.label: Conditions
lessons.3.title: Visiting vehicles are guests that do not connect themselves
lessons.3.summary: Dragon, Cygnus, HTV, and others autonomously approach to the vicinity, but may leave the final connection to the arm.
lessons.3.body.0: Official ISS daily logs repeatedly record the flow where the crew monitors the approach of Cygnus or HTV from the Cupola RWS, captures them with the SSRMS, and then ground robotics control moves them to the berthing position and mounts them on the CBM. The typical division of labor is: capture by the crew, attachment by the ground.
lessons.3.body.1: Approach is conducted using the R-bar or a designated corridor. PROX links, handheld LIDAR, and centerline cameras supplement visual observation. A GO/NO-GO decision is issued only after the arm, docking mechanism, attitude, communications, and abort trajectory are all confirmed.
lessons.3.body.2: Russian-segment vehicles like Progress use a different docking system. Not every resupply vehicle is captured by the Canadian Arm. Check the vehicle type and switch to the appropriate primary arm.
lessons.3.facts.0.label: Typical
lessons.3.facts.1.label: Location
lessons.4.title: The Workstation Is Three Screens and Two Hands
lessons.4.summary: Identical configurations exist in the Cupola and U.S. Lab; most operations require two qualified crew members.
lessons.4.body.0: NASA/TM—2018–220042 officially describes the RWS. The ISS has two identical workstations: one in the Cupola and one in the U.S. Lab (Destiny). Each station features three video monitors, a display control panel, a PCS, a cursor device, and two 3-degree-of-freedom hand controllers.
lessons.4.body.1: Many operations require two qualified on-board operators. M1 operates the arm, while M2 handles procedures, cameras, sensors, and ground communication. Due to ground delay, hand controllers are used exclusively by on-board astronauts, while the ground sends script commands.
lessons.4.body.2: A mini-game where one person views three screens is a simplification. In reality, a colleague's voice provides depth perception. A master of silence would fail at this station.
lessons.4.facts.0.label: Configuration
lessons.4.facts.1.label: Roles
lessons.5.title: Depth Lies to a Single Eye
lessons.5.summary: Arm tip, truss, Cupola window. Synthesize images with different parallax into a single trajectory in your mind.
lessons.5.body.0: Official capture logs list lab RWS camera downlinks, handheld LIDAR, and approach monitoring setups as checklists. Crew members view the real scene through windows and the flat monitor images simultaneously. Relying on only one source leads to a missed grapple.
lessons.5.body.1: Lighting changes every 90 minutes. Manage the whiteout on the day side and black crush on the night side by adjusting exposure and switching cameras. The surface of visiting vehicles changes shape depending on the angle of solar incidence.
lessons.5.body.2: The ground views a different camera set. Even at the same moment, they see different faces. Therefore, words passed to CAPCOM must specify distance, rate, and which camera is being viewed, not just 'close.'
lessons.5.facts.0.label: Onboard
lessons.5.facts.1.label: Ground
lessons.6.title: Dextre Is a Fine Hand, Not a Capturing Hand
lessons.6.summary: SPDM is primarily operated from the ground, carrying tools to handle bolts, valves, and blankets.
lessons.6.body.0: The Special Purpose Dexterous Manipulator (Dextre) is a Canadian dexterous robot. Official Robotic Refueling Mission (RRM) explanations state that ground control equipped Dextre with tools to demonstrate blanket cutting, cap removal, valve operation, and fluid transfer.
lessons.6.body.1: Dextre sometimes sits at the end of the Canadian Arm 2. The long arm carries roughly, while the fine hand touches. It is not used for capturing visiting vehicles. Mixing roles breaks qualifications and procedures.
lessons.6.body.2: RRM explanations note that tools have built-in cameras, LEDs, and fault tolerance. The main battlefield is careful ground scripting, not second-by-second manual control.
lessons.6.facts.0.label: Primary Operation
lessons.6.facts.1.label: Use
lessons.7.title: Capture Is a Chain of Approach, Stop, Grapple, Inspect, and Attach
lessons.7.summary: Treat the official log checklists as pass/fail conditions.
lessons.7.body.0: The official log from January 12, 2014, lists time-stamped steps: ground CBM inspection, SSRMS high hover, crew monitoring and capture from the Cupola, subsequent PCBM inspection, ready-to-latch, CBM bolts, and arm limp and brake. Procedures stop the urge to open the hatch prematurely.
lessons.7.body.1: The HTV-7 log has the same skeleton: approach monitoring, grapple, ground inspection positioning and installation to Node 2 Nadir, followed by external pallet extraction. Even if the vehicle changes, the chain order remains largely the same.
lessons.7.body.2: The mini-game only plays the 'grapple' part of this chain. State aloud that inspection, berthing, and power supply remain after passing.
lessons.7.facts.0.label: Crew
lessons.7.facts.1.label: Ground
lessons.8.title: Stopping Is Part of Arm Skill
lessons.8.summary: Residual relative velocity, loss of visual contact, proximity to a singularity. In all cases, the next command is to stop.
lessons.8.body.0: Human-robot allocation reports distinguish between ground-based operations, which rely on scripts due to latency, and on-board operations, which use hand controllers. Both retain the authority to abort to a safe state in the event of the unexpected. The arm swings large masses and can damage trusses and solar arrays.
lessons.8.body.1: The visiting vehicle also has an abort option: interrupt approach and retreat. Do not pursue with the arm extended. A safe environment is one where two spacecraft can simultaneously declare, 'We are not capturing today.'
lessons.8.body.2: During debriefing, verbalize why the operation was stopped. A simulation that cannot be stopped will result in a delayed stop during the next capture.
lessons.8.facts.0.label: Principle
lessons.8.facts.0.value: If you cannot see it, stop.
lessons.8.facts.1.label: Authority
lessons.8.facts.1.value: Both on-board and ground personnel can abort to a safe state.
lessons.9.title: Arm qualification is a team qualification, not an individual skill.
lessons.9.summary: M1, M2, Ground Robotics, Flight, and CAPCOM. Five parties observe the same approach and add one sentence each.
lessons.9.body.0: The official daily report's completion checklist includes RWS setup, PROX, LIDAR, camera downlink, capture, inspection, CBM, limp, and brake. No single genius pilot can satisfy this sequence simultaneously.
lessons.9.body.1: The candidate course makes robotics mandatory not only for future capture operators. Those who EVA near the arm, allocate power, or yield scientific timelines must also understand the limits of the same machine.
lessons.9.body.2: The badge signifies the ability to read the depth of three screens and achieve a grapple. In the next emergency scenario, you must manage a situation where this arm cannot move—power loss, communication blackout—using other means.
lessons.9.facts.0.label: On-board
lessons.9.facts.1.label: Ground
quiz.0.prompt: Which official mission attached Canadarm2 to the ISS?
quiz.0.explanation: STS-100 (Assembly 6A) prioritized the installation, activation, and inspection of Canadarm2.
quiz.1.prompt: According to official reports, where are identical RWSs located?
quiz.1.explanation: The ISS has identical Robotics Workstations in the Cupola and the U.S. Lab.
quiz.2.prompt: How many video monitors does each RWS have, as officially recorded?
quiz.2.explanation: Each workstation has three video monitors, a DCP, a PCS, a cursor, and two 3-DOF hand controllers.
quiz.3.prompt: Who primarily uses the hand controllers (due to official latency reasons)?
quiz.3.explanation: Due to ground latency, manual operation is limited to on-board personnel, while the ground sends script commands.
quiz.4.prompt: What is the typical division of labor for Cygnus or HTV, as shown in official daily reports?
quiz.4.choices.1: Ground only grabs with hand controllers
quiz.4.choices.3: Dock only in the Russian segment
quiz.4.explanation: Examples often show the crew capturing from the Cupola RWS, while subsequent movement and CBM attachment are handled by ground commands.
quiz.5.prompt: Which is an appropriate primary use for Dextre (SPDM)?
quiz.5.choices.1: Fine maintenance and tool work (primarily ground remote)
quiz.5.explanation: During RRM, ground control equipped Dextre with tools to demonstrate cutting, valve operation, and fluid transfer. It is not used for capture.
quiz.6.prompt: According to NASA reports, what is the number and breakdown of robot arms on the ISS?
quiz.6.explanation: The 2018 official technical report lists three: Canadarm2, Dextre, and Kibo's JEMRMS.
quiz.7.prompt: What does the official chain indicate should be done immediately after capture?
quiz.7.choices.3: Move to inspection position, verify the mating surface, then attach
quiz.7.explanation: Daily reports record the sequence of PCBM inspection, ready-to-latch, and CBM bolting after capture.
quiz.8.prompt: Which combination correctly describes the advantage and trap of having 7 joints?
quiz.8.choices.0: Redundancy for obstacle avoidance and excessive joint velocity near singularities
quiz.8.explanation: Redundant degrees of freedom assist in avoidance, but near singularities (e.g., fully extended elbow), the end-effector's micro-targeting can result in dangerous joint velocities.
quiz.9.prompt: What roles does the official documentation assign to M1 and M2?
quiz.9.choices.1: M1 operates the arm, M2 supports procedures, cameras, and ground communication
quiz.9.explanation: Many tasks require two qualified operators, with roles divided between piloting and support.
quiz.10.prompt: Which is the appropriate way to communicate distance to the ground during capture?
quiz.10.choices.2: Distance, rate, and which camera is being viewed
quiz.10.explanation: The ship and the ground view different feeds. 'Close' without numerical data and visual source does not establish a shared reality.
quiz.11.prompt: What is the next command if relative velocity remains or the target is lost?
quiz.11.choices.3: Stop and lower to a safe state
quiz.11.explanation: For a large mass, the skill is to stop the moment hesitation occurs. The visiting vehicle also has abort and retreat procedures.
quiz.12.prompt: What operation did STS-100 record as a 'first in history'?
quiz.12.choices.0: Robot-to-robot transfer between the Station Arm and Shuttle Arm
quiz.12.explanation: Transferring the cradle from the Station Arm to the Orbiter Arm was recorded as the first robot-to-robot transfer.
quiz.13.prompt: Why is the understanding that all resupply vehicles are captured by Canadarm2 incorrect?
quiz.13.choices.0: Because the arm does not exist
quiz.13.choices.1: Because some vehicles, such as those on the Russian segment, use a different docking system
quiz.13.choices.2: Because no visiting vehicles come to the ISS
quiz.13.explanation: Depending on the vehicle type, autonomous docking and berthing (arm) are distinct. Procedures are switched based on the vehicle.
quiz.14.prompt: Which task is included in those demonstrated by Dextre in the RRM official explanation?
quiz.14.choices.2: Blanket manipulation, caps, valves, fluid transfer
quiz.14.explanation: Ground control demonstrated cutting, opening valves, and ethanol transfer using Dextre and specialized tools.
quiz.15.prompt: What work does the official daily report continue after a successful capture?
quiz.15.choices.3: Joint inspection, attachment, power/bolts, and pallet extraction if necessary
quiz.15.explanation: Capture is a temporary point in the chain. Inspection, CBM, limp/brake, and handling of external equipment continue.
glossary.0.description: A 7-joint station robotic arm used for walking, assembly, maintenance, and visiting vehicle capture.
glossary.1.description: The arm's 'mouth' that secures a grapple fixture with a wire to form a structural connection. Attached to both ends.
glossary.2.description: The hardware on the target side that the LEE grasps. Electric grapples also carry power and data paths.
glossary.3.description: Control stations located in the Cupola and US Laboratory. Equipped with three monitors and two hand controllers.
glossary.4.description: A dexterous robot for fine maintenance. Primarily operated remotely from the ground; not used for visiting vehicle capture.
glossary.5.description: A mechanism that joins pressurized modules or resupply vehicles with bolts. Used in the 'attach' stage after capture.
glossary.6.description: A method of positioning a visiting vehicle to a berthing port with an arm and attaching it with a CBM. The counterpart to autonomous docking.
glossary.7.description: The robotic arm of the Kibo module. One of the three arms on the ISS.
glossary.8.description: The position where the arm waits before capture. After ground preparation, control is handed over to the crew.
